706315.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold”), but this root presents a number of problems, such as the lack of the suffix *-onos in Proto-Indo-European, the lack of any words meaning "chair" from this root in any other Indo-European…

706312.t: Unknown; often compared with the second element of Middle Irish gairb-driuch (“bristle”) and Lithuanian drikà (“threads hanging from the loom”), though Beekes rejects both connections and leaves the origin unknown, noting that the semantic roots used to…

706337.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰurā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door”). Cognates include Sanskrit द्वार् (dvā́r), Latin foris, Old Armenian դուռն (duṙn) and Old English duru and dor (English door) and Russian дверь (dverʹ).

706320.t: From earlier *θύγατηρ (*thúgatēr) (compare with the Homeric accusative form θύγατρα (thúgatra) created to avoid the four syllables of θυγατέρα (thugatéra) and fit the hexameter) via Limitation Law which required the accent to be placed on the last two…

706334.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰūmós, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”). Cognates include Sanskrit धूम (dhūmá), Lithuanian dūmas, Latin fūmus, Old Church Slavonic дꙑмъ (dymŭ) and Albanian tym.

706309.t: Cognate to Sanskrit ध्रणति (dhráṇati, “to sound”), Latin drēnsō, and Old English drān (English drone). Compare also θρέομαι (thréomai, “to cry aloud, shriek”).

706349.t: Likely from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewH- (“to shake, move violently”), though Beekes expresses semantic doubts. Cognate to Sanskrit धू॒नोति॑ (dhūnóti, “to shake; to move to and fro quickly”) and Old Norse dýja (“to shake”).

706342.t: Probably an Anatolian loanword; compare Luwian [script needed] (tuwarsa, “vine”).

706323.t: From θύω (thŭ́ō, “to storm; to rage”), with a suffix by analogy with ἄελλα (ắellă, “whirlwind”).

706300.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *tʰrəsús, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰr̥sús, from *dʰers-. Cognate with Proto-Slavic *dьrzъ, Sanskrit धृषु (dhṛṣú), and Lithuanian drąsùs.

706356.t: Related to Mycenaean Greek 𐀵𐀨𐀐 (to-ra-ke), a technical word without etymology; probably a loan from Pre-Greek or some other substrate, based on the variant θύραξ (thúrax) showing variation ω/υ and the suffix -ακ-.

706322.t: Maybe from θύος (thŭ́os, “burnt offering; incense”), but the concept of a vase for pounding incense is rather strange. According to Beekes, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuH- (“to fly about; to dash”).

706344.t: From θύρα (thúra, “door”) + the root underlying οὖρος (oûros, “watcher, guardian”) and ἐρύω (erúō, “to protect, guard”).
